subtopic: EXPO 86 DISTRIBUTION OF TICKETS TO POLITICIANS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXPO 86 DISTRIBUTION OF TICKETS TO POLITICIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to put on the record the fact that a CP story has confirmed what we in British Columbia already knew, namely, Progressive Conservative MPs from British Columbia have been given 4,100 tickets to give to the public for the opening ceremonies of Expo 86. The New Democrats and the Liberals are splitting four tickets between them.
Expo is going to be a great national festival. Not only will it celebrate the future of British Columbia and Vancouver as the host city, but it will also be a great credit, as Expo 67 was, to the country as a whole. For the Government to convert this into a political extravaganza rather than a national and provincial festival is directly contrary to the unanimity with which people from all three political Parties are approaching this particular event.
I call upon the Government to take politics out of Expo, give it back to the people, and give it back to Members of Parliament across the board.

Mr. Speaker, multicultural organizations across Canada are outraged by recent actions of the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Jelinek). These organizations have provided input to the Government more than once recently on the direction they would like multicultural policy to take. They have indicated shortcomings in Government action on the policy and have asked for more support for their own community acitivities.
While these groups waited for the opportunity to discuss these policy matters, they were suddenly told that the Minister
was developing a totally new multiculturalism policy which was in the final stages of preparation for cabinet consideration. The Minister did not ask for advice on this determination. He did not invite reaction to a draft statement. Instead, he said he was already acting on the new policy and was reviewing the whole funding and granting procedures in line with the development of the new policy. The members of our ethnocultural organizations and communities deserve a better lesson in parliamentary Government than the Minister has provided.

Mr. Speaker, the death of a young Ottawa woman on January 23, 1986, while undergoing a therapeutic abortion, has confirmed what everyone suspected. In many cases therapeutic abortion committees are no more than a rubber stamp.
Erin Shannon's abortion was listed as approved at 8 a.m. even though the committee did not meet until 10 a.m. Her abortion was initiated by 10.05 a.m. Apparently this is not unusual. The committee routinely approves 40 abortion applications at its weekly meetings which last only 20 minutes. That gives about 30 seconds to the consideration of each case.
Under our laws a therapeutic abortion committee should guarantee that a woman contemplating a pregnancy termination has received reliable information about her own and her baby's health, as well as information about the more positive alternatives to an abortion. These factors should also influence the decision of a committee on an application for abortion. This does not happen now, and the entire committee process is a meaningless farce.
I urge Hon. Members of the House seriously to consider changing our laws-

subsubtopic: RESIDENTIAL REHABILITATION ASSISTANCE PROGRAM-APPLICATION REFUSALS IN WINNIPEG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, residents of Winnipeg are angry at the way in which the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program has been unilaterally altered by the Minister responsible for housing. This program has been responsible for regenerating entire neighbourhoods in Winnipeg. Without it and the Core Intiatives Program, parts of downtown Winnipeg could have gone the way of central cities in the United States.
Last year 1,200 homes were rehabilitated under these programs. This year no money has been released as yet. A quarter of the year is thus gone. Winnipegers have warmly endorsed the program and have co-operated fully with it, but now they find their RRAP applications have been cut off because of changes in the income requirements set by the Minister. People with applications dating back as long as two years have been cut off. Forty completed and processed applications, just awaiting CMHC signature, have been turned down. A full 600 of 900 applicants have been disqualified although they acted entirely in good faith, yet the Government will not see fit to judge their applications under the criteria under which these people applied-

subsubtopic: NEEDS OF INDUSTRY IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians were pleased by the decision of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) to award the contract for the building of the new CN ferry to a Canadian shipyard. Now, however, is the time to focus our attention on the urgent needs of the shipbuilding industry in British Columbia. Now is the time to proceed with construction of the promised Class 8 Arctic icebreaker.
The icebreaker will provide important logistic support, and protection of Canadian sovereignty in Arctic waters. It must incorporate the most up to date technology, be efficient, and be built at reasonable cost. All these elements can be delivered by the shipyards in North Vancouver, British Columbia, which are renowned for their expertise in icebreaking technology and utilize the most advanced and productive techniques of design and construction. I hope the Ministers involved in making the decision on the icebreaker will move quickly so that our West Coast shipbuilding industries will have this opportunity to contribute to Arctic development which they so justly deserve.

Mr. Speaker, Dr. Vladimir Brodsky is a Russian physician who has been sentenced to three years in a labour camp for malicious hooliganism. The KGB has offered Dr. Brodsky his freedom if he renounces an independent peace group he helped establish in 1982.
This doctor is guilty of working for peace through association with "The Group to Establish Trust Between the U.S.A. and the U.S.S.R.". This case symbolizes the concern Canadians have for efforts physicians in Canada and other places have made to remove the threat of nuclear war.
Dr. Brodsky's internment relegates the status of Dr. Chazov and his Soviet Physicians for Peace Group to that of a Russian progaganda tool. It ridicules Mr. Gorbachev's peace overtures as being only gestures.
I respectfully request this House and its Members to regard the treatment of Dr. Brodsky as representative of Soviet regard for non-governmental peace groups in Canada, and 1 hope all Members will join me in requesting the Soviet leadership to restore his basic freedoms to Dr. Brodsky.

More Canadians have jobs, more people are buying homes, and more people are seeing an improvement in their standard of living thanks to the implementation of Conservative policies. The National Arts Centre Corporation will implement such cost-saving and revenue-increasing programs as may be required to operate within the financial resources at its disposal, including the recent reduction to its parliamentary appropriation of one million effective April 1, 1985. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate today in third reading of Bill C-62, an Act respecting employment equity which, as has been indicated in previous debate, could be titled the smoke and mirror Bill. Of course the Bill deals with employment equity. It results from the recommendations of Judge Abella in her report released in November, 1984.
Indeed we have come some distance since 1870 when the first two women were employed by the Public Service of Canada and 1882 when the Toronto Labour Council first supported equal pay for equal work. It has been a difficult struggle for many groups. It has been a tiring and long fight for the target groups about whom we are talking, to gain their rights. Of course I am talking about native people, visible minorities, handicapped, and women.
In our view there is no question that the Bill must be strengthened. Bill C-62 requires teeth and some real action. We are disappointed that the Government has not seen fit to accept the many amendments which we proposed to strengthen the Bill. There is no way we can expect movement toward full employment equity unless the federal Government and Parliament set an example. I remind Hon. Members that Parliament is excluded from Bill C-62, which means the House of Commons, the Library of Parliament, and the Senate. The Bill also excludes all Departments and Ministries which fall under the jurisdiction of the Treasury Board as the employer. In our opinion we need a much more comprehensive Bill. It should affect a greater number of employers and employees. It should have real teeth, and real enforcement of employment should be in the Bill. The Bill falls short of the expectations of the target groups for whom it was meant. What seems obvious to us is that it is an advance, but a timid advance.

Mr. Speaker, this less than forward-looking approach with respect to the affirmative action legislation is tantamount to an outright betrayal of the hopes of about 60 per cent of Canadians who expected this Government to come up with a mandatory program to guarantee equity in a society which barely a year ago proclaimed Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, thereby entrenching equality in this country.
Bill C-62 demonstrates again that the Tories talk a good line on fairness but a type of fairness only they can see. Companies,
I remind Members, are not required to submit operational plans for approval or to report specifically about their initiatives to the Minister, or to the agencies responsible for administering this Act. The Minister, of course, can issue guidelines. We all know that, but that is somewhat of a weak position. Nothing in the Bill says that she can apply them, except that she may, if she wants. "We will knock on the door", she said a couple of days ago, and knock again and again and say: "Please put into effect the principle of employment equity".

Mr. Speaker, I would like to re-emphasize something, because we are now at third reading of this Bill which is bound to be passed by the Conservative majority in the House, and we must clearly explain why our position differs from theirs.
The Bill does not contain a clear definition of employment equity. There is no definition, no commitment pertaining to equal pay for equal work, no specific statement on the establishment of the necessary standards or criteria to define obstacles to employment, no guidelines on the removal of discriminatory practices, no methodology, and no date for the implementation of the directives.
Mr. Speaker, Crown corporations and companies engaged in federal work must submit reports within three years. That is what it says in the Bill. Analyzing and consolidating this information can be done by the Minister.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to get back to what I was saying yesterday, about our conviction that the principal employer, namely Treasury Board, the departments for which it is responsible, and Parliament, should be subject to Bill C-62. We feel that in this way, we could set an example to which perhaps the private sector could look for guidance, an example set in good faith. I did a little research last night to find out whether progress had been made with respect to the Affirmative Action Program-step by step or, even better, by leaps and bounds- being implemented in the Canadian Public Service today. As I said before, and I have said it several times, since 1971 Parliament has adopted a number of measures. In 1983, the Liberal Government announced a comprehensive affirmative action plan for the Public Service, for which the President of the Treasury Board would be responsible. Interestingly, things have changed, and a real effort has been made within the Public Service to be fair and to restore a measure of equity to hiring procedures.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention a few statistics. In
1983,	the number of women working for the federal Government, that is, in the federal Public Service of Canada for which Treasury Board is responsible, was 90,816 or 40.6 per cent. In
1984,	92,093 or 41.1 per cent were employed by the Public Service of Canada. In 1985, 92,800 or 41.6 per cent. Mr. Speaker, these increases are not exactly breathtaking-1 per cent, .5 per cent-but they are more encouraging for women and also show that a measure of equity has been established.

However, if we look at a breakdown of the jobs held by women, and I am getting back to this subject because it is interesting, we see that in 1983, Mr. Speaker, out of 90,816 women or 40.6 per cent, only 5.4 per cent were in management positions. In 1984, this figure rose to 7 per cent, and in 1985 a little higher, to 7.8 per cent.
We can therefore say that roughly 8 per cent of employees in management positions are women.
Now if we look at the other end, in the administrative support category, we find out that, in 1983, 82 per cent of employees working as clerks, typists or in other administrative support jobs were women. The percentage rose slightly to 82.6 in 1984 and 82.7 in 1985. So the rising trend is unmistakable.
Therefore, despite public service reductions and Government cut-backs, there have been increases of 0.8 per cent in the number of women in the management group, and 0.5 per cent in over-all employment in the Public Service of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to say that because it is important to have indicators or signs showing where we are headed with respect to employment equity.
Mr. Speaker, I referred to this program to promote hiring and employment, particularly the one concerning women, because I had said in an earlier speech that as far as the handicapped are concerned, for example, everybody knows that Mrs. Suzanne Azziz has been doing a tremendous job under the federal Government program for the handicapped. If my information is correct, close to 400 physically handicapped people have been hired recently by the Public Service Commission and integrated into the system.
But yesterday, Mr. Speaker, I alluded to the systemic resistance which exists even in this Parliament, a resistance which perhaps is not sought or even planned that way, but which is there nonetheless. Excuse me if I get a bit personal, but I would like to talk about the problems the physically disabled have in coming to the House and even working on Parliament Hill, Mr. Speaker. We all know this. We had a demonstration recently when disabled people wanted to come in their wheelchairs. We had trouble getting them into the visitors' gallery. We all know that our elevators are difficult to operate for people with physical handicaps, for instance, people in a wheelchair. Just try and press the button to call the elevator, just try not getting stuck while the doors are closing, when you are in a wheelchair. It is well-nigh impossible, Mr. Speaker.
We even have one interpreter in the House who is blind, and he has been taking our elevators for years without knowing where he is going because no one thought of providing braille or sound in the elevator. These are things we could reasonably expect to be provided by an organization, by a system that claims to have all the latest technology. Mr. Speaker, these things do exist right here in Ottawa.

Last night, I went to see one of my friends, Roger Thibault. His apartment building has an elevator that calls out "up" and "down" and the floor number, and also has braille, for the benefit of people with a hearing or sight disability. However, here in the Parliament of Canada, a public place, a place where we should make it possible for everyone to come and listen and meet the Members, we have yet to install a sensible system or to ask someone to modernize our system. I think this is shocking!
It is quite unacceptable that we should go on like this, that we should not be included in Bill C-62; we are an employer, we have employees here, and I know some of them who find it difficult to work here. We are not fully aware of this because we have not made any special effort to improve the situation. I hope there will now be a movement for us in Parliament to show leadership. The situation is the same in all Government buildings-physical access difficulties, mobility obstacles, and safety problems for the handicapped.
Mr. Speaker, I would rather not spend too much time on this point because I think I have made myself very clear. We must admit there are systemic arrangements, systemic problems which are not necessarily planned that way but which we will have to solve. We will have to find solutions with serenity.
Various statistical studies, some of which were referred to in the report of the Royal Commission on Equality in Employment, provide a bleak picture of employment for women, disabled persons, native people, and visible minorities. They demonstrate, without a doubt, that there is an imbalance, both in statistical and monetary terms. Everyone knows that women earn lower average incomes. It is a fact of life. If one looked at the statistics of the public service one would see that women do not earn the same amounts as their male counterparts for performing, in most cases, similar jobs. There is nothing in Bill C-62 which touches upon that important problem.
Disabled persons suffer from extraordinarily high unemployment rates. When they are employed, they tend to be concentrated in low paying, marginal sectors of the labour market. Added to an already difficult position are expenses which nondisabled workers do not face but are part of the everyday life of disabled people. These include expenses for medication, special aids, and special devices for transportation.
I do not like to say this, but it should be noted that most of the people in the Public Service of Canada who were hired under the program to assist disabled people and to encourage the hiring of disabled people were hired in term positions. When the Government lets people go, the first to be let go are usually term employees who, in many cases, are disabled people. I thought they had acquired a right to work in the

Native people experience a level of unemployment about five times higher than that of the nonnative population. When they are employed, it is usually in the unskilled sectors of the labour market and they have disproportionately low incomes.
Yesterday I referred to the difficulties which landed immigrants have in adapting to the two official languages of the country. We must review our programs of language training and we must ask the provinces to co-operate. Judge Abella reported on this extensively. She said that we must do something to modernize the methods and to make those courses more acceptable so that new Canadians will have less difficulty advancing in the workforce. In my riding landed immigrants frequently fill the lowest paid jobs in the lowest skilled sectors. They are usually the most vulnerable because their jobs are the first to be abolished in tough times.
From a purely economic point, employment equity is needed to ensure that human resources are not wasted because of discriminatory practices. A healthy economy needs the contributions of all qualified people who are willing to work and are competent. That is the only judgment we should make-not whether they are native, handicapped, disabled, or women. If they are competent they should be allowed to compete and to obtain jobs. The exclusion of women, visible minorities, disabled people, and native people from job opportunities and benefits can only contribute to the high cost of social service programs.
In conclusion, we are disappointed with the Government's refusal to amend this Bill. We would like to have had included in the Bill a higher penalty, and have it relate to the action plan as well as the reporting clause. We would like to have seen the penalty at $500,000. We would like to have had the designated groups which speak strongly for the disabled, the native people, and women's groups included in this Bill so they would be consulted when things need to be improved.
We would have liked to have had a better definition of "reasonable accommodation". The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised the handicapped people that he would study this issue personally. He did not study it very long or hard and he did not do a darn thing about it. We would have liked a requirement that the action plans be sent to the Minister for review and be available to the Canadian Human Rights Commission, upon request, for examination.
We would have liked those things to have been included in the Bill but, unfortunately, they are not. The Bill will be accepted as it is, but it is a smoke and mirrors Bill. Everyone in the House accepts the principle of the Bill, but its lack of teeth frustrates us. We would like to have had a Bill with more power and equity. We would like to have had a stronger Bill.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) has made a good speech. He is a good Member of Parliament and a very progressive one. However, I
wonder why the Liberal Party did not do this during its 20 years in power. His party formed the Government in 1963 under Mr. Lester Pearson with 168 seats in the House. It then came to power once again under Mr. Pierre Trudeau. My question, therefore, is this: Why did the Liberal Party do nothing in 20 years to ensure employment equity in Canada?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy that the Hon. Member has asked this question because it gives me a chance to point out that it is quite untrue to suggest, as do the Parliamentary Secretary and the Conservative Party, that we did nothing. It is completely untrue, and I would like to remind the House that, in 1971, Canada was the first country in the Western world to recognize the role of women at the highest level of Government by creating a Cabinet position for the advancement and promotion of women.
A non-governmental advisory council on the status of women was established in 1973. In 1972, the Federal Government endorsed the convention of the World Labour Organization on equal pay for work of equal value. The Liberal Government also introduced an omnibus Bill to ensure equal status for women in 1975. In 1976, we gave passage to the Canadian Human Rights Act, which forbids discrimination based on sex. In 1978, we amended the Canada Pension Plan to provide for the equal sharing of retirement credits, as well as the Canada Labour Code to eliminate pregnancy as a motive for lay-off or firing. Then, in 1982, we had in this very House a debate of nearly one year on the famous Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which was finally passed by Parliament after being introduced by the Liberal Government and in which Section 15 guarantees equality for all Canadians. Afterwards, we also created the Abella Commission because this issue had to be examined. The Abella Commission was therefore established in 1983 and it presented its report in 1984.
Unfortunately, the Canadian public decided to throw us out, and I am not blaming anyone. However, the Government in power certainly had lots of advice. Now I have been in the House for at least fourteen years now, and we have been discussing the subject for at least that long. That is my answer, and that is what I said three or four times in this House, and if I am asked the same question again, I will repeat my answer once more.
Since 1971, Mr. Speaker, a lot has happened here. We took care of native people, we took care of housing, we took care of the disabled, we took care of women. Projects and programs were set up. I am certainly not ashamed to say it. I am not saying that I am satisfied with what was done. I didn't say that. I didn't say I was satisfied. I merely said, Mr. Speaker, that I am one of those people who believe that by doing a lot more we will get a lot further in this area and get there faster.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should begin by suggesting, with all due respect, that you have the time mechanism, which I know you keep in front of you, checked for any faults it might have, because that was certainly the longest 10-minute comment period that I have experienced since it came into being.
I want to say that the now standard tactic of pointing out, and quite rightly, the inconsistencies between what Liberal members of the House now say about employment equity-and for that matter about a great many other subjects-and what was actually done while the Liberals were in power, is fair ball.
It is also fair, I suppose, to note that many of these issues are issues which evolve over time, and that Governments respond to the degree of social consensus that develops around issues. I say this, not in defence of past Liberal Governments, but to point out that I think the social and political consensus for affirmative action developed long before the Liberals had
April 23, 1986

the opportunity to be defeated, an opportunity they so richly deserved and took advantage of in 1984.
Long before 1984 the consensus had been created that it was time for real employment equity in this country, and real affirmative action. We went so far not so long ago as to enshrine in our constitution a reference to affirmative action, which highlighted that as a mechanism for bringing about greater equality in this country. I do not think, with all due respect to the individual and local initiatives that the Member from Ottawa-Vanier pointed out, the Liberal Party can be let off the hook for the lack of action which it demonstrated with respect to this particular issue while it was in Government.
I want to say also that I think it is a good time to reflect on what 1 suppose is tragically common in the political life of this country, and perhaps others as well, and that is the gap, sometimes a horrendous gap, between promise, expectation and reality. In August, 1984 the then Leader of the Opposition and now Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said, and I quote:
Our party will ensure that companies providing services to the federal government hire increasing numbers of women to perform such services. When seeking government business, these companies will be required to detail their action plans, timetables, and programs for attracting, training and advancing women within their operations . .. We support the need for human resources planning within the federal bureaucracy, which includes goals and objectives to achieve parity for women, at all levels of Government operations, commensurate with their skills and expectations.
Numerical goals are one of the several goals required: training and retraining are others.
That was offered to the Canadian public by our current Prime Minister when he was running for office in 1984. The result of that rhetoric, which was part of an over-all and considerably transparent election strategy, was to promise everything to everybody. The Conservatives in 1984 were going for broke. They were not going to offend anybody. Whatever you wanted, they were on your side. If you did not want to test the Cruise missile, neither did they. If you wanted to test the Cruise missile, so did they. It did not matter what your position was you could find a Tory who would respond positively to your feelings and to your concerns.
This Bill has become an example of the disappointment and the cynicism which that kind of election strategy, however successful-and certainly no one would argue about the success of it-eventually results in. There was an expectation with respect to this issue that the Government would live up to its promises in this regard, an expectation that has been sorely violated by the reality of the legislation that we have before us. We can quote now from Beryl Potter of the Coalition on Employment Equity for Persons with Disabilities the following statement:
Like the bill-it's not even worth the paper it's written on-I've never been so disillusioned in my life as I am with Prime Minister Mulroney. I was a supporter of him. I worked for him in his campaign and I am totally, totally disillusioned.
A good example of the gap between promise, expectation created and promoted by the Conservative Party, and now the disappointment that comes with legislative reality, is the fact that the Progressive Conservative Government has not been
Employment Equity
willing to respond to a social consensus that is already there. It is not as if the Conservative Party was being asked to do something terribly radical. I feel, as I think others feel, that for some time we have been at a point in our social and political thinking where governments could afford to move on this without any great danger to themselves. We have to ask ourselves the question, why does the Progressive Conservative Government, having taken the trouble to devise legislation and to cause the House of Commons to debate this for many, many hours, not take the trouble to do the job right while it was taking the trouble to do the job at all?
I think the reason for that is that when the Conservatives got into the business of promising everything to everybody as an electoral strategy they were involved in contradicting themselves at a great many turns, particularly when they made the kinds of promises they made with respect to employment equity, as well as in some other areas. I say that because I do not think any member of the Conservative caucus would deny that they have a fundamental commitment to the market-place as the arena where certain kinds of decisions are made, indeed, where a great many important decisions are made as far as Progressive Conservatives are concerned, and where those kinds of decisions ought to be made according to Progressive Conservatives. The Progressive Conservatives believe that the market-place is the final arbiter of who will get what job, how they will be paid and organized, et cetera.
When the Progessive Conservative Party promised employment equity, it was either unconsciously engaged in a form of intellectual self-contradiction or it was consciously misleading Canadians about what was intended. In the final analysis, I believe the Progressive Conservative Party was true to its own principles.
While that is understandable, it should have been honest enough to say long ago that the ideal of enforced employment equity in the market-place, which these groups have called for, was against its fundamental principles about how the economy should run. A proper democratic debate could then have occurred.
There could have been a real debate in this country about how our economy should be organized and what should be properly left to the market-place and what should be properly accomplished through the enforcement mechanisms that these groups and the New Democratic Party have been calling for. However, that debate has not taken place because the Progressive Conservative Party decided in 1984 that it would not have any real debate. The Conservatives were going to keep their cards close to their chests and would indicate to the public only that which it wanted it to know.
We have discovered that the Conservatives did not mean what they were saying, that our criticisms of the Conservatives over the years have been correct. The fact is that the Conservative Party is not capable of acting against the wishes of the business community in this country. Clearly, that is the

rationale behind the weakness of the legislation before us today.
That unwillingness is evident in other areas as well. Recently, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), who I see listening intently, I hope, talked about the insurance industry and complained that many groups were putting themselves in risky situations because they could not afford to renew their insurance. Member that nothing will be done in this and other areas of concern unless the Government musters the political courage to take on some of the institutions that it is in the habit of defending. For example, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) had an incredible trust in the oil industry which I do not believe has been matched by action. She assumed that as world oil prices decreased there would be a corresponding, complementary and timely reduction in energy prices at the pumps.

However, if the companies do not meet certain requirements of this Employment Equity Bill there is a $50,000 fine in some cases. Big deal! It is quite clear that many of the companies we
are concerned with are wealthy enough to regard $50,000 as simply the cost of doing business.
Employment equity is being dealt with in much the same way as the financial institutions, the oil industry and the insurance industry. Furthermore, the Liberals have had much the same philosophy. We were told for years not to worry about the environment. We would be told that the Minister of the Environment had talked to the industries involved, who volunteered to monitor themselves to ensure that they would not do anything wrong. We have seen this incredible naivety over and over again about how these institutions will behave when it comes to their own self-interest. It is time that we realized that we will have to take steps to enforce those things we want to see happen, whether it concerns the protection of the environment or affirmative action for employment equity. The Government has not been willing to do that. That is why this Bill has been so ridiculed by the very people who had such high expectations for it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to continue debate on third reading of Bill C-62. We have been trying as hard as we can to make this a meaningful Bill that would fulfil the hopes and aspirations and needs of the people it is supposed to serve. This Bill is suppose to meet the needs and concerns of women, native people, the disabled and handicapped and visible minorities.
There are certain Tory partisans who have recently lamented the determined stand taken by the Opposition to get Bill C-62 amended so we can achieve its alleged purposes. These partisan Tories complain because Members of the Opposition care about the plight of their fellow man. They lament the fact that we are making an effort here in the House to convince the Government to do something to improve Bill C-62. I am proud to rise as often as I can to plead the case of those groups. I am proud that in this House of Commons we can call to the attention of the Government the plight of those groups to whom it made promises. Over half of our population are women. We have a large number of native people. The handicapped and disabled represent approximately one eighth of the population. Estimates from Statistics Canada tell us that one in every eight Canadians is disabled. All of those who belong to minority groups, especially the visible minorities, are worth talking about. A very large part of our population seeks protection. Therefore, the time we spend on this Bill is not wasted if we can somehow persuade the Government that there is much it can do to improve the Bill.
The alleged purpose of Bill C-62 is to achieve equality in the workplace so that no person shall be denied employment opportunities or benefits for reasons unrelated to ability, and to correct the conditions of disadvantage in unemployment experienced by women, aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities and persons who are, because of their race or colour, in a visible minority in Canada. Those are the alleged objectives of this Bill. Those partisan Members of Parliament
April 23, 1986

who criticize our efforts to try to have the Bill achieve its purpose betray their lack of genuine human compassion for those groups who wait for some move forward. I suggest that these critics should perhaps ponder the words of the great British poet, John Donne who many centuries ago wrote words which ought to remind us of the importance of compassion. John Donne was also the Dean of St. Paul's Cathedral in England. He said, and I quote:
No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main; if a clod be washed away by the sea, Europe is the less, as well as if a promontory were, as well as if a manor of thy friends or of thine own were; any man's death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind; and therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls: it tolls for thee.
It is a basic premise of our culture and underlying civilization that we are concerned about the plight of our fellow man. There is not one person in the House of Commons who can be sure that he or she will not tomorrow be part of one of those groups, if they are not already. Certainly not one single Hon. Member, male or female, can negate the possibility that he or she may be struck down in such a way that there would be limitations, handicaps or disabilities. No one is exempt. Everyone in this country can be protected and must be protected by law but this law does not protect them. Everyone is a potential victim and needs this kind of protection. No one is an island unto himself and no one should feel exempt from the strictures of this concern.
Let us look at one important group, the disabled and handicapped. Let us look at those people who have skills, who can work and who want to work but who cannot work because they cannot get work because their disabilities are viewed as being too grave. And who makes that arbitrary decision? It is the arbitrary opinion of those who interview these disabled and those who do not even give them the opportunity to be interviewed. The employer may feel in his or her arbitrary opinion a particular disabled person cannot function well in the office or plant because the necessary accommodation for that disabled person is not available, and the employer feels there is no requirement to solve that "problem". At the present time those people who are disabled have to live with the arbitrary opinion of an employer as to whether or not they can fit into the company's plans.
We look in vain in Clause 2 for any definition of what constitutes a disabled or handicapped person. This Bill is faulted. Does this Clause mean that the employer has only to make sure that a certain percentage of disabled persons- which is set by the employer himself-must be hired? The employer can decide what constitutes disability. Is that a sprained arm, a disability which is mild or is it a serious disability? The disabled came here to find the answer. They came to the committee which discussed this Bill and tried to explain that it was important for some kind of idea to be given of what is intended. More importantly, they wanted to know what is meant by the words "reasonable accommodation".
Clause 4 of Bill C-62 states that an employer shall implement employment equity by instituting such positive policies and practices and making such reasonable accommodations as
Employment Equity
will ensure that persons in designated groups achieve a degree of representation in the various positions of employment. The Bill says that designated groups will be able to have reasonable accommodation. That is the goal. But representations of one eighth of our population came to the committee and asked that some kind of idea be given as to what the Government meant in its legislation by "reasonable accommodation" so that employers when they read this law would have some idea of what the Government had in mind. We agree that one cannot set forth everything of what might be meant by "reasonable accommodation" as interpreted by various companies which might be involved. Pathetically, of course, there are not very many companies which might be involved in this legislation in any case. This Bill is a sham.
The handicapped groups have asked for some kind of definition of reasonable accommodation in the legislation. Amendments were put forward proposing that definition. The Opposition proposed these amendments in complete good faith, feeling that the Government would be very pleased to see a way to meet the concerns of those groups that came to represent the one-eighth of the population who are disabled and handicapped. An amendment was proposed with a definition so that employers would understand what the Government meant by this legislation.
We proposed to define reasonable accommodation as including, without restriction so that it could cover other situations as well, the reasonable adaptation of the workplace, hiring practices or the job description to accommodate the needs of designated groups including the special needs of a qualified disabled person through a provision for physical accessibility, assistive devices, flexible job design and modification and human support services. We asked the Government to include this proposal in the legislation at the request of all the groups representing handicapped people. We proposed it in committee and we again proposed it here in the House. Both times the Government rejected such a simple definition or guideline that would give employers the understanding of what this legislation is supposed to be trying to achieve.
The failure of the Bill to give any examples, never mind guidelines, of what is meant by reasonable accommodation is a grave flaw in the Bill. One must therefore conclude that there is a lack of seriousness and sincerity in the Government's attempt to come up with legislation that will be effective. Not only can the disabled not refer an employer to a guideline for what is meant by persons with disabilities or reasonable accommodations, but they can see that nothing will actually happen as a result of the passage of this Bill.
What will happen if this Bill is passed? Look at it from the point of view of someone who is handicapped. We should put ourselves in the place of a person who has seen progress through the decades toward the hope that through the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the Human Rights Commission, and now an attempt to bring about employment equity, he will

April 23, 1986
Employment Equity
have a chance to get a job. The handicapped no longer want to wait. This tempting carrot has been put in front of them. They hope that we will at last bring about legislation that cares about them and responds to their needs. Elowever, they ask how they will know that they will be able at last to get jobs.
What do the handicapped find that this legislation will do for them? Clause 4 indicates that the employer is supposed to eliminate barriers to employment or promotion for the handicapped. As well, the employers are supposed to institute policies and practices to ensure that persons in the various categories will be able to have something done for them. That employers are now supposed to do that according to law does not change a thing because they are already supposed to do that. We do not need to pass a law to say that there shall be equality for all in this country because, according to our human rights legislation, that is how it stands now.
What does this Bill add? Does it bring anything new to employment equity? It tells companies that they are supposed to treat people equally. My heavens, that is what the Charter of Rights and Freedoms already tells employers. It already tells every employer in the country, never mind the few to which this Bill refers, that they are supposed to treat people equally. This Bill again tells them the same thing. How does that help the people who are disabled and handicapped? The Bill is telling employers what they already know.
The proof that this Bill does not work is that nothing is happening to change systemic discrimination against handicapped people. That is what Judge Abella said in her report and that is why she said that something must be done to eliminate systemic discrimination against, for example, the one-eighth of the population who are handicapped or disabled.
If it were the case that all the Government need do is pass a Bill with no teeth in it and everything would be all right, then why does the Government not behave that way itself? What kind of trust can the disabled and handicapped have in the Government when they know, as I said in the House of Commons on March 17, that the vast majority of disabled persons employed by the Public Service Commission in 198485 were employed in limited or term positions? Now with the Tory Government cut-backs, the Government will be even more prone to put the handicapped in limited and term positions. What hope is there that the Government will make this law any more effective than the Government's present policies for the handicapped? If its present policies do not serve the handicapped and the disabled, then how can they count on this law which has no teeth in it to serve them any better?
I wish I could proceed with this discussion because there are other points about Clauses 5 and 6 which also indicate that this legislation lacks teeth. Before I close, I wish to mention that the only provision for which a penalty is attached under this Bill is the provision that an employer file a report. An employer can report anything, as long as he files a report he is okay. He will be subject to a penalty only if he does not file a report. What is the leverage of this fine? The employer is
liable to a fine not exceeding $50,000. The fine could be no dollars, it could be $5 or it could be $100 but it is not necessarily $50,000.
Why has the Government brought this legislation forward? It has brought it forward in order to make people think that it is doing something about employment equity. It has brought it forward to fulfil a symbolic gesture, all the while knowing that the corporate sector will know that it is a toothless and absolutely meaningless exercise. It is nothing but an exercise on the part of the Tories in political cynicism and hypocrisy.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my friend in the Liberal Party. I have before me a copy of the study of the Economic Council of Canada entitled "Women Reentering the Labour Force and Training Programs, Evidence from Canada". The Hon. Member made a very progressive speech; it called for various changes. However, this report indicates that our employment policies over the years have not done enough to promote women into non-traditional occupationa areas and that there has been discrimination for years in Government policies for women.
I should like to quote from the report wherein the following is indicated at page 43:
Moreover, in 1983-84, the federal Government spent over $200 million on apprenticeships and industrial training-Women are almost entirely absent from apprenticeships. They are under-represented in the industrial training program (in proportion to their presence in the labour force), and they train in predominantly female occupations.
Further on the same page, the following is indicated:
EIC should designate target occupations for training women and should develop training programs for women in these occupations jointly with employers. The target occupations should be occupations where there is a strong demand for qualified workers; these occupations might be drawn from the CTST and the ONI.
The report really condemns many of the programs of the past in terms of them not really being fair to women, discriminating against women and not steering women into nontraditional occupations. Why was the Liberal Party, which was in power over 20 years, so lax at trying to open up new job opportunities for women? Why did this discrimination continue for so many years despite the fact that the Liberal Party was in power? Why was the Liberal Party so late in realizing that women were discriminated against? Why did the Liberal Party not do something about it when it was in power?
I think the report is a good one in that it condemns the lack of Liberal action over 20 years in terms of being fair to women. What does the Hon. Member have to say about that?

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to appear in any way as simply trying to be defensive by saying that everything the Liberals have done in this regard was perfect or rosy. I ask the Hon. Member not to assume that that is what I am trying to say. On the other hand, it would behove my hon. friend to listen to the comments about and the examples of the impressive Liberal record over the years which were made
April 23, 1986

earlier. If he had listened to that review, he would have learned that it was impressive. However, I am trying to point out that we have made a logical progression in terms of the steps we have taken.
An attempt to bring forth a Bill at this point which is purely symbolic is heartbreaking for those, of whatever Party or sympathy, who await the decision of the House of Commons on Bill C-62. It would be better if the Hon. Member, with only 30 members in his caucus, would concentrate on what the Conservative Government is doing and on its responsibilities. It would be a good idea for him to attempt to get the Government to improve the legislation. However, if he wants to spend his time taking shots at the Liberal Party, he can do so, if that is spending his time in the best way. From my point of view he would be better advised to try to persuade the Government to improve this particular piece of legislation for the sake of the people who need this help. I do not know whether he has done that in his question or comment.
In any case, I am pleased that his Party agrees with the Official Opposition that the legislation is not adequate and does not meet the alleged goals which it seeks to achieve. I am deeply disappointed that the Tory Government is in effect trying to give the impression that it is doing something by passing this piece of legislation when I know that it has almost no impact upon the parties or groups affected.

Mr. Speaker, I have a general question because I have a lot of respect for the Hon. Member. He is an ordained minister of the church as well. Could he comment upon whether or not other organizations are doing enough to promote equity among different groups? For example, I have often said that farm organizations should involve more women in their operations. Of course, we cannot pass legislation to that effect, and I am not suggesting it, but I have often suggested that there should be more women in the leadership of farm organizations and trade unions. Personally I am very happy, for example, that the next President of the Canadian Labour Congress will almost certainly be Shirley Carr. These are steps in the right direction. Would the Hon. Member agree that the same should apply in some of our churches and that they, being tremendous institutions and great moral leaders, could set a better example by having more women in their hierarchies?
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) directed a similar question to me yesterday.
I was not here.

I think the Hon. Member's question is a justified one. All groups, particularly the churches, have a moral responsibility to provide leadership in this area, not only in terms of their own employment policies but in terms of teaching and preaching the fact that all men are equal before God. I think that can be said by anyone of any faith and should be continually emphasized.
Employment Equity
The Hon. Member is right in indicating that it is not enough to say: "Do as I say but not as I do". If the Hon. Member is suggesting that there is hypocrisy involved in every group, I agree with him. We in the Liberal Party are proud of the fact that our President is the Hon. Iona Campagnolo. However, when we look at the number of Members of Parliament sitting in the House, we are unhappy that we do not have more women who are Members of Parliament. Everyone has a responsibility. In terms of our own home life, we should reexamine our attitudes toward women, native people, and the handicapped. Certainly it is a responsibility of the church.
I believe the Hon. Member's question concerned the Anglican Church. The Anglican Church should forthwith approve the consecration of women as bishops. It has decided to ordain women as priests, which is a logical step. The Government should move as quickly as possible to make meaningful the policy of eliminating systemic discrimination as the Bill is supposed to do. However, I fear-and I am sure the Hon. Member would agree-that this is not happening.

Mr. Speaker, I was glad to hear the Hon. Member say what he said, and I should like to ask him a question which might be quite radical for this institution dominated by males. He mentioned that there were very few women in the House of Commons. All three political Parties at the federal level, and certainly at the provincial level in different sections, have parity clauses in their constitutions visa-vis gender. Often half the delegates must be female. For example, half the delegates to national or provincial council meetings must be female. We have seen that practice internally within our Parties. Would it be too radical to suggest that perhaps we should have legislation wherein half the Members of the House must be women? In other words, there could be dual ridings, approximately 180 such ridings. Each riding would elect two Members, one of whom must be a woman. Would the Hon. Member agree with that proposal? After all, all three political Parties are moving in that direction internally. Is it too radical a suggestion in terms of this very staid and conservative institution?

Mr. Speaker, it is a proposal which I have heard proferred by other people. Having given thought to the matter, it seems that the principles involved in this piece of legislation would indicate that finally we are dealing with the fact that people must have merit to be given jobs. I think the same applies to the electorate. If the electorate deems there are certain people it wants to elect, then whether they are male or female is not the issue. The issue is the quota. I think we can discuss this further perhaps privately.
I would like to conclude on this note, Mr. Speaker. The need, if you will, for an effort to recruit women is something which is very much in the minds of political Parties, at least it should be. Rather than put down quotas which might limit the number of women later on because then there would have to be a certain number of men, and when you figure women

April 23, 1986
Employment Equity
constitute 51 per cent of the population, that gets a little too much into the numbers game, perhaps we can discuss it at a further time.

Mr. Speaker, we have no wish to cut off this debate. This matter has been before the House and committee for some time. All those who wanted to be here were here ready to debate. speechtext: On the same point of order, Mr. Speaker. I think that the question has not been put, nor has it been completely read, and as long as the question has not been read, if my interpretation of the Standing Orders is correct, a Member can still seek the floor, which is what happened in the case of the Hon. Member for York-West (Mr. Marchi).
Who was recognized.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Indeed, he was given the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Both Member are correct. The Parliamentary Secretary is correct when he said that the question was called. The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) says that the question was not put. The question was not put. Therefore, the Hon. Member has the floor for debate.
Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat surprised that government Members would have such an objection to listen to further debate.
You were surprised in the lobby.

Yes, I was in the lobby. Yes, I had an interest and that interest is genuine, and that is why I am on my feet right now. If there is genuine interest on the other side to debate and improve this piece of legislation, I would think that, following my intervention, we will see the Parliamentary Secretary and the quasi-Minister of National Defence get up on their feet to defend the position in Bill C-62, and I challenge the Minister to do that.
I would like to participate in this debate once again. I have been involved from the beginning, commencing with second reading, then in committee, at report stage, and several days ago when the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), my colleague, moved an amendment, I spoke then. Several days ago I said that the debate and the process were frustrating. If you were a Member of Parliament and a participant throughout the entire process you would have to ask yourself about this Bill, as we are and as community individuals from the four target groups, for whom the legislation is intended, Mr. Speaker. We have seen, particularly at committee stage, group after group after group of women, the disabled, native people and people representing the visible minorities. They came before the committee and stressed the need to improve and strengthen Bill C-62. We saw participation at second reading once it was known across the country what Bill C-62 contained and, more important, what Bill C-62 did not contain.
The four target groups, the four community-based action groups, did not come before us simply as a one-time wonder. Very many of these same organizations came before this Parliament and this House of Commons during the constitutional debate when we were discussing the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. They came before the Abella Commission, which set out very courageously and progressively, I might add, a vision for Canadians in terms of equal opportunity in the workplace. They came before the Equality Now hearing, they came before the Equality for All hearing, and they also came before the committee that looked into the handicapped which published the Obstacles Report. In each and every single case they came at great expense, great energy and effort to articulate to their leadership at the federal level, to you and me, Mr. Speaker. They told us what it meant for them to be discriminated against either on the basis of sex, handicap or the colour of their skin. They tried to articulate in a very sensitive and effective manner what it was they needed from this House in terms of legislation and leadership for them to be freed from this type of bondage.
As Members of Parliament we have dealt and continue to deal in this House with these frustrations. We do so in our constituencies when we meet them. One of the basic elements of frustration we encounter is the question of employment.

People continuously seek the advice and assistance of Members of Parliament to help them find employment. These are people who have been in the unemployment lines for days, months and, in some cases, years. We should be cognizant of the fact that it is a great frustration, and it is that because in Canada and throughout the world people measure their self-worth and selfdignity in relation to a job. Somehow having a job fulfils one's goals and aspirations, keeps families intact and families on the go.
If we can admit to the fact that not having a job is very serious, then who are we to say to those individuals who are denied a job, not because an opportunity does not exist but because of a handicap, their colour or sex, or because of native cultural backgrounds? These people are Canadians. They are not some foreigners, they are not some new Canadians or some immigrants-and I am not suggesting we discriminate only against those classes-but they are Canadians like you and I, Mr. Speaker. They deserve an equal opportunity. They deserve an equal slice of the Canadian pie. In their estimation, they are not getting it. That is why they came before this House during debate on Bill C-62 to inform the Government that the Bill will not deliver equality but will merely speak to equality. That is not good enough. They came before this House and told the Government, "We don't want to be carted out on some kind of platform as one of the four target groups come election time and hear said: 'Look what we did for the natives. Look what we have done for the visible minority Canadians in this country'". They are not gullible. They are not naive. They do not want to be hoodwinked and, more important, they do not want other Canadians to be hoodwinked into believing that the lot of these Canadians is being improved, because it is not.
Member organizations within these four target groups have said very clearly to Parliament that they would rather have no Bill than have Bill C-62 in its present form. They are frustrated after having stated their position to the Government year after year, through report after report, and seeing no action. If Bill C-62 contained some decency and some movement on their complaints, recommendations, and representations to the committee, they would have been pleased. They would have accepted that as a first step. However, there has been no movement. There has only been talk and rhetoric. That is why they are displeased. Everyone in the House believes in equal opportunity. We should not accept a piece of legislation which does not do that which it purports to do. Rather than do that, we should transcend Party politics and work hard to deliver a piece of legislation which will do what it is intended to do.
My colleagues and I do not stand in our places to oppose simply for the sake of opposing, and not simply to debate until six o'clock. We are taking a position of principle. For years members of these four target groups have been telling the Government what they want. At the eleventh hour we at least wish to take the opportunity to articulate those concerns. Bill
Employment Equity
C-62 is simply not good enough, and the four target groups do not wish to accept it.
We have done more than simply talk. Through our critic we moved 36 amendments which would have given Bill C-62 strength and effectiveness. We recommended that the committee and the Government accept these amendments in order to demonstrate decency and moral integrity. One would have expected that one, two, or three of those amendments would have been accepted in good parliamentary faith. However, none of them were accepted. The amendments which we proposed came from the four target groups.
For whose benefit is this legislation being put forward? Is it for Members of the House or for the viewing audience? Of course not. If our purpose is to create equality in the country for the four target groups and those groups are not satisfied with this legislation, why is the Government prepared to proceed with it? Why is the Government so anxious to have this legislation passed? Why has the Government censured every member of this Party who has spoken on Bill C-62? We are not out of order. We make no apologies for debating this issue in the House. We do not apologize because we are trying to be the lightning rod between the four target groups and the federal Government. We will not apologize today or tomorrow.
